title: Design a URL Shortener
summary: A full framework walkthrough of a bit.ly-style service: estimates, base62 math, four ways to generate short codes, caching the redirect path, 301 vs 302, and async click analytics.

questions.prompt: Should a URL shortener redirect with **301** or **302**? What do you gain and lose with each?
questions.hint: Which one can the browser cache?
keyPoints: 301 Moved Permanently can be cached by browsers, so repeat clicks may not reach our servers
301 reduces load but loses click analytics and makes deleting or expiring links unreliable for users who cached it
302 Found (temporary) sends every click through our servers
302 enables analytics and link changes at the cost of more traffic; choose based on requirements

questions.prompt: Your shortener will create **500 million** links per year and keep them for **10 years**. How many base62 characters do the codes need at minimum? If you use **7** characters with random codes, what's the chance a new random code collides with an existing one at the end of year 10?
keyPoints: Total links: 500M × 10 = 5 × 10^9
62^5 ≈ 9.2 × 10^8 is too small; 62^6 ≈ 5.7 × 10^10 is enough, so the minimum is 6 characters
With 7 characters, P(collision per new code) ≈ 5 × 10^9 / 3.5 × 10^12 ≈ 0.14%
Handle collisions with a conditional insert and retry
questions.answer: `5×10^9` links. `62^5 ≈ 9.2×10^8` (too small), `62^6 ≈ 5.7×10^10` (enough) → **6 characters** minimum. With 7: `5×10^9 / 3.52×10^12 ≈ 0.14%` per attempt, so retries are rare.

questions.prompt: Write `encode(n)` and `decode(s)` for base62 using the alphabet `0-9a-z A-Z` (in that order). What does `encode(3843)` return?
questions.hint: Repeatedly take `n % 62` for the last digit and divide by 62. `3843 = 61 × 62 + 61`.
keyPoints: encode: loop while n > 0, prepend ALPHABET[n % 62], set n = Math.floor(n / 62); handle n = 0
decode: for each character, n = n * 62 + ALPHABET.indexOf(ch)
decode(encode(n)) === n round-trips
encode(3843) is "ZZ" (61 is 'Z', the last character)

questions.prompt: Compare three ways to generate short codes: **truncated hash of the URL**, **global counter + base62**, and **Snowflake IDs**. Which would you choose for a URL shortener and why?
questions.hint: Consider collisions, coordination, length and guessability.
keyPoints: Truncated hash: deterministic and dedups identical URLs, but truncation causes collisions that require check-and-retry
Counter + base62: no collisions and shortest codes, but needs coordination (use range allocation per server) and is guessable unless scrambled
Snowflake: no coordination and time-sortable, but a 64-bit ID needs up to 11 base62 characters, too long for a short link
Clear choice with justification (e.g. counter with range allocation and a reversible scramble, or random codes with conditional insert)

questions.prompt: A celebrity tweets one of your short links and it gets **50,000 clicks per second** for an hour. Your redirect service reads from Redis, falling back to the database. What could go wrong, and how does your design cope?
questions.hint: One key, one cache shard. And think about analytics writes.
keyPoints: A single hot key lands on one cache shard, which can be overloaded (hot key problem)
Mitigations: replicate hot keys to multiple cache replicas, an in-process local cache on redirect servers with a short TTL, or serve the redirect from the CDN/edge
If the key expires or the cache misses, many requests may hit the DB at once (thundering herd); use request coalescing or keep hot keys from expiring
Click events go to a queue asynchronously, and aggregation prevents 50k DB writes per second for counters
Redirect path stays independent of analytics so a slow pipeline doesn't slow redirects

questions.prompt: Extend the design: users want a **dashboard** showing clicks per link per hour, broken down by **country**, for the last 90 days, updated within 5 minutes. The service averages **4,000 clicks/s**. Design the analytics pipeline and estimate its storage.
questions.hint: Store raw events or aggregates? How many rows does an hourly aggregate produce?
keyPoints: Redirect servers publish click events asynchronously to a durable log/queue (e.g. Kafka) partitioned by link code
A stream processor aggregates counts per (code, hour, country) in windows and writes them to an analytics store (time-series or columnar DB), meeting the 5-minute freshness
Volume: 4,000/s × 86,400 ≈ 350M raw events/day; at ~100 bytes each ≈ 35 GB/day of raw events, which can go to cheap object storage for reprocessing
Aggregates are much smaller because rows depend on active (link, hour, country) combinations, not clicks
Handle duplicates and late events (idempotent aggregation, allowed lateness), and expire data after 90 days
